Summer break. What comes to mind when you think about summer break? For students, that might mean a road trip with family, a trip with friends to a Caribbean island, or even sleeping the days away and occasionally waking up to eat and watch Netflix. The last thing on a students mind is school work. While it is vital for students to keep their knowledge intact with summer projects, this shouldn't take time away from having their summer break. If teachers were to design these projects with specific directions and interesting topics, students wouldn't have to waste time on a project that is most likely meaningless to them. Students should be given teacher-designed projects over the summer so that students take proper safety precautions, stay within the topic of the class, and don't spend too much time on a single project for one class.

Parents play a big part in these projects because they are the only ones there to make sure that safety is a top priority during the course of the project. Safety needs to be a big concern when students are given projects so that the teachers don't end up getting in trouble for something that they didn't have any control over. When given directions, students will follow them according to how they were stated to ensure they are scored properly after the project is completed and turned in. Students do very well on assignments when given directions and a rubric to follow because it gives them a standardization as to what the teacher is looking for in the assignment. If a student had too much freedom with the project, they wouldn't have these directions to follow, which could potentially lead to numerous disasters. Having the students follow certain protocols will help ensure that the student stays safe whether the project is as simple as handwriting an essay or as complex as creating chemical reactions.

A typical school schedule consists of four to eight different classes for every student. Now imagine what it is like to have that many different projects over summer break when a students time is supposed to be their own. When a student takes time to themselves, they often don't think about what is going to happen at school the next year or even anything relatively related to the topic of school. Having the teacher create a project will allow the student to stay on topic within the courses curriculum, restricting students to only learn the topics necessary for that specific course. This will keep all unnecessary topics and ideas out of the project to keep all assignments short and precise.

As a high school student myself, I know that it is very easy to over think something when not given rules, guidelines, or directions to follow. Students tend to over think things when given too much freedom which, in turn, leads to wasting valuable time that could've been used for another classes project or even just spending time with family and friends. When an assignment takes too much time, stress starts to be introduced into the picture. Students undergo enough stress during the regular school year already, and don't need to go through more over their time that is supposed to be used to take a break from school. Some may say that students need to learn time management and that having the freedom to choose their project will help them to gain experience with the important life skill. The weakness in this statement is that summer should not be spent worrying about projects that aren't supposed to take forever to complete. Yes, there should still be projects so that students don't lose what they learned in prior classes, but it shouldn't be a burden on the students time with family and friends over their summer break.

At the beginning of my high school experience, I was given a student-designed project with the task of figuring out what pH level E. coli bacteria grew best in. My instructor didn't give me any safety precautions or notices that I should have done something differently. Because of this, the chemicals that I was storing rotted away at the containers they were in, and ate away at the paint on my dresser. For this reason, I now take extra precaution when I'm working on a student-designed project because I don't want to be stuck in the same situation again. Not wasting time and keeping everyone happy and safe should always be taken into account when a student is given a teacher-designed project. Teacher-designed projects are, in the end, more beneficial for the student and for the teacher.

Drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle. There are several important reasons for this. 

First and foremost, using a cell phone while driving is a serious distraction that puts the driver and others on the road at risk. When a driver is focused on a cell phone conversation or text, their attention is diverted from the critical task of safely navigating traffic. This can easily lead to lapses in awareness of their surroundings and slower reaction times. Numerous studies have shown that driving while distracted by a phone is as dangerous as driving drunk. 

Second, cell phone use requires at least one hand to be occupied and takes the driver's eyes off the road. Even hands-free conversations or voice commands divert mental focus from driving. Operating a vehicle demands the full and undivided attention of both hands on the wheel and eyes on the road ahead. Any distraction from a cell phone introduces dangerous possibilities of accidents.

Third, texting while driving is especially risky because it involves taking both hands off the wheel and eyes completely off the road for prolonged periods. Texting drivers are completely unaware of traffic conditions and unable to respond to any sudden dangers. This extreme form of distraction from cell phones has been a cause of many devastating accidents. 

In conclusion, cell phones present too much of a distraction in any form while a person is responsible for safely operating a vehicle. The risks of accidents and harm are just too high to allow any cell phone use behind the wheel. Drivers need their full attention focused on the task of navigating traffic safely without outside distractions. For this reason, cell phone use should not be permitted for drivers. Public safety depends on keeping drivers' hands on the wheel and eyes on the road.

The Benefits of Limiting Car Usage  

Many communities throughout the world are becoming increasingly dependent on cars for transportation. However, there are advantages to curbing overreliance on personal vehicles. Limiting car usage can both benefit the environment and improve quality of life.

One of the major upsides of restricting car travel is that it leads to reduced pollution and emissions. According to a study conducted in London, decreasing private car journeys by just 10% would cut transport greenhouse gas emissions by over 200,000 tons per year (Source 1). When fewer motor vehicles are on the road, there is less fossil fuel burned and less pollution emitted into the air. This lowers health and environmental costs associated with vehicle emissions. 

In addition, restricting car usage encourages active transportation methods like walking, cycling, and public transit. A report from Vancouver found that residents drove 30% less after the city made infrastructure improvements for cyclists and pedestrians (Source 2). Shifting modes of travel in this way delivers public health gains. Regular physical activity like biking or walking to destinations can help reduce rates of lifestyle diseases. It also makes communities more vibrant as more people experience their neighborhoods by foot rather than from behind the windshield.

Finally, limiting personal cars means less traffic congestion and demand for parking. Source 3 notes that in Manhattan, where alternatives to driving are readily available, traffic moves faster despite having more people and activity compared to car-dependent cities. With fewer vehicles clogging up limited street space, commuters benefit from reduced travel times whether using public transit, walking, biking, or driving. This saves costs associated with time lost in traffic as well as expenses to build additional roadway and parking infrastructure.

In conclusion, curbing overreliance on personal cars produces environmental, public health, and quality of life advantages for communities. Restricting car usage encourages sustainable transportation methods and a more efficient use of limited urban space. By informing citizens about these benefits, more supportive policies can be enacted to realize these gains.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote. As you know, the Electoral College is a system in which each state is allocated a certain number of electors, based on its population. The candidate who wins the popular vote in a state receives all of that state's electors. This system has been in place since the ratification of the Constitution in 1788, but it is increasingly out of step with the values and ideals of our democracy.

One of the main arguments in favor of the Electoral College is that it protects the interests of small states. Under a popular vote system, candidates would only need to campaign in the most populous states, and the needs of smaller states would be ignored. However, this argument is no longer valid in the 21st century. With the advent of modern technology, candidates can easily communicate with voters in all 50 states. In fact, many of the most successful presidential campaigns in recent years have been run by candidates who have focused on building a national coalition of support, rather than focusing on a few key swing states.

Another argument in favor of the Electoral College is that it prevents a few large states from dominating the presidential election. However, this argument is also flawed. The Electoral College actually gives more power to small states than they would have under a popular vote system. This is because each state, regardless of its population, is guaranteed at least three electors. This means that a voter in Wyoming has more than three times the voting power of a voter in California.

The Electoral College is also undemocratic. Under this system, it is possible for a candidate to win the popular vote but lose the election. This has happened five times in American history, most recently in 2016. In this case, Hillary Clinton won the popular vote by nearly 3 million votes, but Donald Trump won the Electoral College and became President. This is simply unacceptable in a democracy.

For all of these reasons, I urge you to support abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote. This is the only way to ensure that every vote counts and that our democracy is truly representative of the will of the people.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,

In 1976, Viking 1, a spacecraft, was in search for its sister ship, Viking 2. When searching, they snapped photos of various Martian landmarks including what is now known as "The Face on Mars." They took this photo from an angle where it look as if a face was coming out of the ground. At first, NASA thought this might possibly be an artifact from Martian civilization, but were disappointed when they found it was just another landmark. Conspiracy theorists believed NASA was simply trying to hide the truth from them, but all of NASA's research proves the face is just an unusually shaped landmark.

Viking 1, the initial spacecraft to spot the landmark, didn't have the best technology. compared to today's technology, the picture would be considered blurry and out of focus. Yes, at first a few scientists believed the face was an alien artifact, but instead of jumping to conclusions, they did more research. this meant another spacecraft would be sent to get better evidence.

On April 5, 1998, NASA sent the Mars Global Surveyor to get the better quality pictures to conclude their research. At this point in time, the technology had improved tremendously and the picture turned out ten times sharper than the first picture taken by Viking 1. As an eighth-grade student, it is common for individuals to begin thinking about their future careers. While making a decision at a young age may seem beneficial, there are also drawbacks to consider. In this essay, we will analyze the benefits and drawbacks of deciding on a career at a young age, including job availability, economic stability, parental ability to cover costs, and the potential impact on mental health and personal growth.

One benefit of deciding on a career at a young age is that it allows individuals to have a clear direction in life. Knowing what they want to do early on can help them focus their education and work towards their goals. Additionally, it can provide a sense of purpose and motivation to work hard in school and pursue opportunities that align with their chosen field. This can lead to a greater sense of satisfaction and fulfillment in life.

However, there are also drawbacks to consider. One major drawback is that job availability may not always be guaranteed. The job market is constantly changing, and certain careers may become obsolete or have limited opportunities. Additionally, economic stability can be a concern, as some careers may have higher salaries or job security than others. It is important for individuals to consider these factors and have a backup plan in case their chosen career does not pan out as expected.

Another potential drawback of deciding on a career at a young age is the impact on parental ability to cover costs. College tuition and other expenses can be significant, and it is important for parents to be able to support their children's education and career goals. If an individual chooses a career that requires a lot of education or has a low starting salary, it may put a strain on their parents' finances. It is important for individuals to consider the financial impact of their career choices and make sure they are feasible for their families.

Finally, there are potential impacts on mental health and personal growth to consider. Choosing a career too early can lead to feelings of pressure and anxiety, as individuals may feel like they have to make a decision that will define their entire lives. Additionally, if an individual chooses a career that they are not passionate about, it can lead to feelings of dissatisfaction and a lack of purpose in life. It is important for individuals to take the time to explore their interests and passions before making a decision about their career.

Should schools have a longer summer break, a shorter winter break, and a week off in the spring and fall? While some people argue that students should have a year-round school schedule with shorter breaks, I believe that students benefit from a longer summer break. A long summer break allows students to travel, spend time with their families, and work in the summer, all while still learning and experiencing new things.

One of the main benefits of a long summer break is the opportunity to travel. Traveling to a new country can be a life-changing experience, and it can be done without worrying about missing school. Students can explore new cultures, learn new languages, and experience things that they may never have the chance to otherwise. Traveling is not just about having fun, it's about expanding one's horizons and gaining new perspectives.

Another benefit of a long summer break is the chance to spend time with family and friends. Summer is a time when students can plan vacations with their loved ones, regardless of whether they attend the same school. Families can create lasting memories together, and students can catch up with old friends and make new ones. Spending time with family and friends is important for everyone's well-being, and a long summer break allows for this.

Finally, a long summer break can also be a great opportunity for students to work in the summer. Many students take on summer jobs to earn money for college or to gain work experience in their field. A long summer break allows students to have enough time to find and secure a job, and to work hard enough to save money for the upcoming school year. This can be especially beneficial for students who are studying abroad, as they may not have the opportunity to work during the school year.

In conclusion, while some people argue that students should have a year-round school schedule, I believe that a longer summer break is the best choice. A long summer break allows students to travel, spend time with their families, and work in the summer, all while still learning and experiencing new things. It's a time when students can recharge, have fun, and return to school ready to learn and grow.

When it comes to important matters in life, seeking guidance from experts and authorities can be a valuable resource. However, there are also potential drawbacks to relying solely on the opinions of others. In this essay, I will analyze the pros and cons of seeking guidance from experts and authorities for important matters in life.

One of the main advantages of seeking guidance from experts is that they have a wealth of knowledge and experience that can be valuable in making informed decisions. Experts can provide insights and perspectives that may not be immediately obvious to the average person, and can help individuals navigate complex issues with greater ease. Additionally, experts can often provide guidance on how to avoid common mistakes and pitfalls, which can save time and resources in the long run.

However, there are also potential drawbacks to relying solely on the opinions of experts. For example, experts may not always have a complete understanding of the individual's unique circumstances and needs. This can lead to incorrect advice or recommendations that may not be the best fit for the individual. Additionally, experts may be biased or have a vested interest in certain outcomes, which can lead to conflicts of interest and potential harm to the individual.

Another potential disadvantage of seeking guidance from experts is that it can lead to a lack of personal growth and development. When individuals rely too heavily on the opinions of others, they may not take the time to think critically and make decisions based on their own values and beliefs. This can lead to a lack of complete understanding of one's life, and can make it difficult to navigate complex issues in the future.

On the other hand, making mistakes can be a valuable learning experience. When individuals make mistakes, they have the opportunity to reflect on what went wrong and learn from their experiences. This can help individuals develop critical thinking skills and become more resilient in the face of challenges. Additionally, making mistakes can lead to personal growth and development, as individuals learn to take responsibility for their actions and make better decisions in the future.

In conclusion, seeking guidance from experts and authorities can be a valuable resource for important matters in life. However, it is important to be aware of the potential drawbacks and to approach guidance with a critical eye. By considering the pros and cons of seeking guidance, individuals can make informed decisions that balance the need for expertise with the importance of personal growth and development.

Limiting car usage has become a topic of discussion in recent years due to efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and create more sustainable communities. While cars have long been the linchpin of suburban life, there are several advantages to reducing car usage and promoting alternative modes of transportation.

One advantage of limiting car usage is the significant reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. According to a study cited in Elisabeth Rosenthal's article "In German Suburb, Life Goes On Without Cars," passenger cars are responsible for 12 percent of greenhouse gas emissions in Europe and up to 50 percent in some car-intensive areas in the United States. By reducing the number of cars on the road, we can drastically decrease these emissions, contributing to a cleaner and healthier environment.

Another advantage is the improvement in air quality. In the article "Paris bans driving due to smog," Robert Duffer explains how Paris enforced a partial driving ban to clear the air of pollution. The ban resulted in a 60 percent decrease in congestion and an improvement in air quality. By limiting car usage, we can reduce the amount of air pollution and create cleaner and safer cities.

Limiting car usage also promotes more sustainable and compact communities. In the article "In German Suburb, Life Goes On Without Cars," Rosenthal discusses Vauban, a car-free community in Germany. In Vauban, street parking, driveways, and home garages are generally forbidden, and car ownership is restricted to two large garages at the edge of the development. This promotes a more walkable and bike-friendly community, where stores are placed within walking distance, reducing the need for long commutes and reliance on cars.

Furthermore, limiting car usage can lead to a decrease in traffic congestion and improved efficiency of transportation systems. In Andrew Selsky's article "Car-free day is spinning into a big hit in Bogota," he describes how millions of Colombians hiked, biked, or took buses to work during a car-free day, leaving the streets free of traffic jams. This not only reduces the time spent in traffic but also improves the overall efficiency of transportation, making it easier for people to travel to work and other destinations.

In conclusion, there are several advantages to limiting car usage, including the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, improvement in air quality, promotion of sustainable communities, and decreased traffic congestion. By actively promoting alternative modes of transportation and creating car-free or car-restricted zones, we can create a more environmentally friendly and efficient transportation system. It is important for individuals, communities, and governments to recognize the benefits of limiting car usage and work towards implementing policies and infrastructure that support sustainable and accessible transportation options.

As it shows in the article "In German Suburb, Life Goes On Without Cars", towns or cities like the experimental town of Vauban, Germany, are capable of continuing life without the added stress of owning a car and lowering the greenhouse emissions caused by them. Although the majority of the citizens do not own a vehicle, there are about 30 percent who do, and those who don't, either ride a bicycle or on what little amount public transportation there is. Out of the 70 percent of Vauban's families that do not own a car, 57 percent sold theirs to move there.

Areas all around the world are beginnig to do the same as Vauban. Creating areas that do not require vehicles mainly due to the amount of greenhouse gas emissions that are causing the majority of the worlds climate change. Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote.

As you know, the Electoral College is a body of electors established by the United States Constitution, constituted every four years for the sole purpose of electing the president and vice president of the United States. The electors are chosen by each state, in a manner directed by the legislature thereof. Each state's number of electors is equal to the number of seats it has in the U.S. House of Representatives plus its two senators.

The Electoral College has been a source of controversy since its inception. In 2000, for example, Al Gore won the popular vote but lost the election to George W. Bush when Bush won a majority of the electoral votes. This has happened five times in American history, and it is likely to happen again in the future.

There are many reasons why the Electoral College is an outdated and undemocratic system. First, it gives more power to voters in small states than to voters in large states. For example, a voter in Wyoming has three times as much power as a voter in California, because Wyoming has three electoral votes and California has 55 electoral votes.

Second, the Electoral College encourages candidates to focus their campaigns on a handful of "swing states" that are up for grabs. This means that voters in other states are effectively ignored by the candidates.

Third, the Electoral College is vulnerable to fraud and manipulation. In 2000, for example, it was revealed that many Florida voters were wrongly purged from the voter rolls, and that some ballots were not counted. This could have changed the outcome of the election.

For all of these reasons, I believe that the Electoral College should be abolished. The President of the United States should be elected by a majority of the popular vote, as is done in most other democracies. This would ensure that the President is elected by the people, rather than by a small group of unelected electors.

I urge you to support a constitutional amendment that would abolish the Electoral College and elect the President by popular vote. This would be a long overdue reform that would make our democracy more fair and representative.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,

I am writing to express my view that the United States should change from the current Electoral College system to instead elect the president by popular vote. While the Electoral College was designed with the aim of giving smaller states more influence, today's system promotes outcomes that do not align with the overall will of the American public.  

The current system can result in a president being elected despite losing the nationwide popular vote. This has occurred a few times in history, with most recent examples being in 2000 and 2016. While opponents argue this helps give small states attention, it undermines the principle of one person, one vote. It means that in certain swing states receives disproportionate attention, while many other states are ignored. This is counter to democratic ideals of equal representation.

It could be argued that the popular vote system could lead candidates to only focus on urban areas. However, campaign strategies would still require appealing to a wide range of demographic and geographic groups. Candidates would still require votes across many states to win a majority nationally. Moreover, campaign funds are better spent trying to persuade swing voters anywhere rather than focusing on narrowly targeting swing states. 

A switch to the popular vote might increase voter turnout as more citizens in non-swing states would feel their votes truly matter in determining the outcome. Currently, many feel their votes do not count based on their state's typical leaning. This could have the effect of increasing civic participation and strengthening representative democracy. 

While changing to a popular vote system may require amending the Constitution, it has the potential to create outcomes that better reflect the overall will of the people. The fast growth of urban areas also diminishes the original rationale of giving small states added influence. For these reasons, I believe the country would be better served by electing presidents based on total national popular vote. Thank you for your consideration of this issue.

Standardized tests have been a part of school life for many years, but the question remains, are they a true measure of a student's abilities? In my opinion, standardized tests are not an accurate way to measure a student's abilities.

First of all, standardized tests are often biased towards certain groups of people. For example, some tests may be written in a way that is more accessible to students from certain cultural backgrounds, while others may not. This means that students who are not part of those groups may be at a disadvantage, even if they are just as smart or capable.

Another reason why standardized tests are not accurate is that they only measure a narrow range of skills. These tests typically focus on reading, writing, and math, but there are many other important skills that are not tested. For example, they do not take into account a student's ability to think creatively, work well in a team, or solve problems. These skills are just as important as reading, writing, and math, but they are often overlooked.

Furthermore, standardized tests put a lot of pressure on students. Many schools and teachers place a heavy emphasis on these tests, which can make students feel anxious or stressed. This can lead to students doing poorly on the test, even if they are capable, simply because they are too nervous.

Finally, standardized tests do not take into account individual learning styles. Every student learns differently, and these tests do not account for that. Some students may learn better through hands-on activities, while others may learn better through reading and writing. Standardized tests do not accommodate these differences, which means that some students may be at a disadvantage, even if they are just as capable as their peers.

In conclusion, standardized tests are not an accurate measure of a student's abilities. They are biased, narrow, and put a lot of pressure on students. They do not take into account important skills, individual learning styles, or the many different ways that students learn. Instead of relying on these tests, schools should focus on providing a well-rounded education that includes a variety of subjects and learning styles. This will help ensure that all students have the opportunity to reach their full potential and show their true abilities.

The use of facial recognition technology like the Facial Action Coding System in the classroom to read students' emotional expressions could provide both benefits and drawbacks. 

On one hand, this technology may help teachers gain insight into how students are feeling during lessons. If a system could detect that many students appear bored or confused by a topic, it may prompt teachers to find more engaging ways to explain difficult concepts. Identifying active negative emotions like frustration could also allow teachers to address issues that are impeding learning for individual students. Over time, analyzing emotional patterns may help personalize learning approaches to better suit each student's needs and keep more of them engaged.

However, this type of constant emotional monitoring could potentially invade students' privacy and make them feel uncomfortable. Young people especially may feel uneasy knowing a computer is scrutinizing their facial expressions throughout the school day without their consent. Students may also worry that a technology focuses too much on emotions rather than academic performance, or that teachers could misinterpret what facial signals actually mean in different contexts. There is also a risk that a reliance on such a system could distance human interaction between teachers and students, reducing the interpersonal relationships that are so important for learning. 

Overall, using facial recognition technology in the classroom presents both opportunities and challenges that require careful consideration. If implemented respectfully with students' privacy and well-being in mind, it could provide some insights. But teachers should not come to over-depend on such a system at the expense of developing close relationships with their students through open communication and observation of each individual. More research would also be needed to fully understand how these systems interpret the complexities of human emotions and social situations in an educational environment.

The Natural Formation of the Face on Mars

Many people see unusual patterns in everyday objects and landforms. When images of the Face on Mars were first captured, it understandably sparked interest about the possibility of an ancient civilization once living there. However, upon closer examination, the evidence strongly suggests the Face is simply a natural rock formation sculpted over time by wind and other erosive forces. 

There are a few key pieces of evidence that support the Face being a natural landform rather than an artificial structure. First, high resolution images reveal no definitive artificial structures anywhere near the Face that would indicate an intelligent source. If it were part of a complex, one would expect to see buildings, roads or other signs of habitation. Additionally, the Face lacks symmetry, which is uncommon for constructed faces or monuments. Its features are uneven and distorted, more characteristic of random geological patterns. 

Second, scientists have identified the specific geological processes that could have shaped the Face's appearance. The rock layers in that region are composed of harder and softer stones. When winds erode the softer layers more quickly than the harder stone "eyebrows" above, it creates shadows that resemble eyes. Over millions of years of steady erosion, such natural weathering could plausibly produce a passing resemblance to a human face. No artificial mechanisms would be needed to explain its formation. 

Lastly, multiple unmanned missions have provided ample opportunity to capture the Face from different angles and lighting conditions. Yet none have revealed any other site characteristics typical of an inhabited settlement. If it were an ancient statue or memorial, we would expect to find other constructed elements nearby over time. The preponderance of evidence thus indicates the Face on Mars is simply a chance product of natural geological forces, not an artifact of ancient Martian civilization. While speculation about its origins is part of human nature, the most scientifically sound conclusion is that it is a natural rock formation, not proof of past life on the red planet.

The ethical debate over the use of animals in scientific research is a complex issue that requires careful consideration. While some argue that animal testing is necessary for medical progress and scientific advancement, others believe it is cruel and unnecessary. In this essay, I will argue against the use of animals in scientific research.

Firstly, animal testing is often inhumane and causes unnecessary suffering. Animals are subjected to painful procedures, such as force-feeding, injections, and exposure to toxic substances, without any form of pain relief. For example, in cosmetic testing, rabbits are often used to test the safety of products such as shampoo and makeup. These tests involve dripping chemicals into their eyes, causing severe pain and discomfort. Such practices are not only cruel but also raise serious ethical concerns about our treatment of animals.

Secondly, animal testing is often unreliable and ineffective. Animals have different physiological and genetic makeup than humans, which means that results from animal testing may not always apply to humans. For example, a drug that appears safe and effective in animals may have adverse effects on humans. Furthermore, alternative methods, such as cell cultures and computer models, have been developed that provide more accurate results without the need for animal testing.

Lastly, there are ethical alternatives to animal testing that can be used in scientific research. These include in vitro methods, such as using human cells and tissues, and non-invasive techniques, such as MRI scans and ultrasound. By using these methods, researchers can obtain accurate results without causing harm to animals.

In conclusion, the use of animals in scientific research is cruel, unreliable, and unnecessary. Alternative methods that do not involve animal testing should be used instead. It is our responsibility to ensure that scientific progress is made ethically, without causing harm to animals.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my strong support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the president of the United States by popular vote.

The Electoral College is a system that was devised in the 18th century and is no longer fit for purpose in the 21st century. Under the Electoral College, each state is allocated a certain number of electors, based on the number of representatives it has in the House of Representatives plus its two senators. The candidate who wins the popular vote in a state wins all of that state's electoral votes, with the exception of Maine and Nebraska, which award their electoral votes proportionally.

This system is deeply unfair. It means that a candidate can win the popular vote but lose the election, as happened in 2000 and 2016. It also means that candidates have no incentive to campaign in states that are already decided, as they know that they will not win any electoral votes there. This results in a two-tiered system, in which some states are effectively ignored by the candidates.

The Electoral College also gives an unfair advantage to small states. A voter in Wyoming has three times the voting power of a voter in California, simply because Wyoming has three electoral votes and California has 55. This is because each state has a minimum of three electoral votes, regardless of population.

The Electoral College is also undemocratic. It is a system in which a small number of people, the electors, can decide the outcome of the election, even if the majority of voters have voted for a different candidate. This is simply not acceptable in a democracy.

I urge you to support abolishing the Electoral College and electing the president by popular vote. It is the only way to ensure that all voters are equal and that the president is elected by the will of the people.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

When it comes to advice, who should we ask? Some of us may have a best friend or a trusted adult that we talk to about certain feelings, but maybe seeking advice from multiple people is more beneficial. Talking to different types of people gives others the opportunity to view things from different perspectives. Perhaps, the person giving advice has already been in that situation. Or, someone disagrees with the advice a specific person gives. There are many reasons to get opinions from more than one person.

Different types of people will, of course, have different opinions, perspectives, and thoughts on the advice they are asked for. Religious beliefs, logic, and their environment, will all play an important role for their answer. For example, the advice seeker's mother most likely won't have the same answer as their father. And a police officer wouldn't have the same ideas as a chemist. Ideas can vary from person to person.

Another idea to expand on, is the fact that others may have already experienced what the advice seeker is asking about. For instance, someone who has never been to an amusement park is nervous about the different rides and ask their friend, who has visited the place many times, whether they should be afraid or not. They tell them it can be a bit scary at first, but after the second or third time, they'll get used to it. That would be an example of how getting advice from others with experience is a good idea.

The last reason to seek advice from a large range of people, is because a disagreement could occur. Looking at advice from another perspective can be a positive experience, but there could always be a chance the advice seeker does not agree with the person giving the advice. A solution to this would be observing how others would react to the situation, and getting an overall view of how they should handle it. There's even a possibility that they rethink what the first person told them because they also disliked the other advice they were given.

So, in conclusion, advice can be seen from many different viewpoints. Certain factors, such as religion, the logic that person uses, and how they grew up, all affect the way someone thinks, resulting in a different answer than, say, the next door neighbor. It's good to be able to find and communicate with people who have already been in the situation, that way, it makes looking for the right answer much less difficult. Though, there are also times when an advice seeker just doesn't agree with the answer they are given. In that case, having different people to share and receive ideas with is important not only the advice seeker, but the advice giver.

The Development of Driverless Cars

While driverless cars present many potential benefits, their widespread adoption also raises serious safety and ethical concerns that require careful consideration. According to the article "Driverless Cars are Coming," autonomous vehicles could reduce traffic accidents by taking human error out of the driving experience. However, they may also struggle with unpredictable situations that human judgment handles instinctively. Overall the technology remains untested on a large scale.  

A key benefit discussed is reduced accidents, as the article notes that human error causes over 90% of crashes. Driverless cars use sensors and software and should not face issues like distraction, drunkenness or fatigue. Yet many edge cases may confuse even advanced AI. Unexpected obstacles like fallen trees after storms may be tricky to recognize without experience. Pedestrians or animals moving erratically could also vex sensors. While accidents may drop on highways, more complex scenarios in cities remain challenging to program for.

Moreover, ethical dilemmas abound. In a crash situation, should the car aim to protect its passengers no matter what, even if it means harming others? How do programmers assign relative values to different lives in such a calculation? Without perfect foresight, accidents may happen due to losing control or system failures. The legal liability in these situations also requires definition.

Overall the technology holds promise if developed prudently. More testing in controlled environments and with backup drivers can help identify shortcomings. Regulations must also anticipate ethical questions and assign responsibilities clearly. While driverless cars may offer future benefits, their risks require thorough consideration and oversight to avoid unintended consequences on public roads. For these reasons, a cautious approach that factors in both promise and perils seems wisest.

Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones in Any Capacity While Operating a Vehicle 

In today's society, cell phones have become nearly indispensable for communication and access to information. However, the ubiquitous nature of cell phones has also led to significant risks when used while driving. There are several compelling reasons why drivers should abstain from using cell phones in any way when operating a motor vehicle.

First and foremost, the act of driving requires a person's full attention and focus. Any distraction while driving can potentially lead to accidents that endanger not only the driver but also other people on the road. Talking, texting, or otherwise interacting with a cell phone diverts the driver's eyes from the road as well as their hands from the steering wheel. Even seemingly simple tasks like checking notifications or changing the music can be dangerously distracting at high speeds. 

Scientific studies have shown that driving while using a cell phone reduces reaction times and situational awareness to similar levels as drunk driving. In fact, data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration indicates that cell phone use is a leading factor in car accidents annually. Texting while driving in particular makes a driver 23 times more likely to be involved in a collision. With so much evidence that phones impair driving ability, the risks are simply too high to justify their use behind the wheel.

Allowing any cell phone use also makes it difficult to enforce more restrictive policies against texting or handheld phone conversations. Drivers may claim they were just changing songs or accessing maps when seen on their phones by law enforcement. A total ban creates a clear standard and eliminates loopholes and arguments over what activities are truly "hands-free." 

In summary, the dangers of cell phone distractions while driving far outweigh any perceived importance of access to phones. For the safety of all citizens that share the road, drivers must abstain from cell phone use entirely when operating a vehicle. Public safety should be the top priority in deciding responsible policies around this issue.

Dear Principal, 

I am writing to you regarding the proposal to require all students to perform community service. While helping the community is certainly a noble goal, I do not think making it mandatory is the right approach. There are better ways to encourage volunteerism that do not take away student's free time.

Requiring community service risks making it feel like a chore or punishment rather than something done out of genuine care and interest. When volunteering is mandatory, it loses the spirit of selflessness. Students may resent being forced to give up their free hours and may half-heartedly go through the motions only to fulfill the requirement. This does little to foster a lifelong attitude of service. 

Instead of mandating service, the school should cultivate volunteerism through other means. Clubs and extracurricular activities that involve helping others could introduce more students to service and allow them to find causes they are passionate about. Recognizing top volunteers with awards can also motivate students without obligation. Leading by prominent example, such as having teachers perform notable acts of service, inspires students to follow naturally. 

While the intent is to teach responsibility to the community, requiring service has the potential for unintended negative consequences. Students' free time is important for rest, hobbies and simply being young. Forcing them to sacrifice that could breed resentments. A voluntary approach where service stems from personal commitment, not duty, is more likely to have lasting impact.

In conclusion, the noble goals of community involvement are better reached through guiding students to choose service willingly, not by mandating their time. I encourage the school to foster volunteerism through choice, recognition and moral leadership instead of obligation. This will instill lifelong values of compassion more effectively.

Thank you for considering my perspective. Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Sincerely,
[Your name]

While summer is meant as a break from the regular school routine, having some structured learning over the summer can help students maintain important skills and knowledge. When given the choice, I believe summer projects are best when student-designed rather than teacher-designed.

When students have autonomy in choosing their own summer project topics, they are more motivated to engage in meaningful learning. By allowing students to pick subjects they find genuinely interesting or relevant to their lives, they will be internally driven to explore the topic in depth. This type of intrinsic motivation leads to better focus and quality of work compared to assignments chosen by teachers without student input. 

Giving students ownership over project topics also fosters independence and skill development. By guiding their own work, students learn valuable skills like time management, decision making, and self-directed learning - skills that will serve them well in higher education and careers. Trying to complete a task completely of their own design also builds confidence facing open-ended challenges.

Of course, some guidance is still useful to ensure projects have educational merit. Teachers could provide general parameters like the type of final work (essay, presentation, etc.) or subject area but leave the specific focus up to students. This balance of student choice within guidelines maximizes engagement while maintaining academic standards.

In conclusion, when the goal is to sustain learning over summer break, student-designed projects are ideal. By letting students follow their interests with some guidance, they are intrinsically driven to dive deeply into self-directed work - an approach that serves their development far better than topics assigned externally. Autonomy, motivation and skill-building will better prepare students for future challenges compared to rigid, teacher-driven assignments over break.

Libraries have been a crucial part of our society for centuries, serving as a hub for knowledge and learning. However, with the advent of the digital age, some people argue that libraries have lost their relevance. In this essay, I will argue against this notion and highlight the continued importance of libraries.

One of the primary reasons why libraries are still important is their role in providing access to information. Although the internet has made it easier to find information, not all information is freely available online. Libraries provide a wealth of resources, including books, journals, and databases that are not accessible otherwise. Additionally, libraries offer a quiet and focused environment for studying and research, which is often difficult to find at home or in other public spaces.

Another significant role that libraries play is in promoting literacy and lifelong learning. Libraries offer a wide range of books, including fiction, non-fiction, and children's books. This exposure helps to develop reading skills and a love for reading, which is essential for academic success and personal growth. Moreover, libraries often host author readings, book clubs, and other events that promote literacy and encourage people to engage with literature.

Libraries also serve as a community hub, providing a space for people to come together and connect with one another. They often host events, workshops, and classes on various topics, such as cooking, art, and technology. This not only fosters a sense of community but also promotes personal growth and development.

Moreover, libraries are essential in promoting equity and access to information for all members of society. They often provide resources and services for underprivileged communities, such as free access to computers and the internet, job training programs, and language classes. This helps to bridge the digital divide and ensures that everyone has access to information and opportunities.

In conclusion, libraries continue to play a vital role in the digital age. They provide access to information, promote literacy and lifelong learning, serve as a community hub, and promote equity and access to information. While the internet has certainly made information more accessible, libraries offer a unique set of resources and services that cannot be replicated online. Therefore, it is essential that we continue to support and fund our libraries, ensuring that they remain a vibrant and essential part of our society.

Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones in Any Capacity While Operating a Vehicle

Operating a motor vehicle requires a driver's full attention at all times. However, with the rise of cell phone ownership, many drivers have begun using their phones even while driving. This dangerous distraction puts both the driver and other people on the road at risk of accident or injury. For this reason, drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity when driving.

There are several reasons why cell phone use while driving is too great a distraction. First, cell phones divert a driver's eyes from the road. Even brief glances away from the road to check a phone can cause a driver to miss important visual cues like traffic signals, pedestrians, or other vehicles. Second, cell phones divert a driver's mental focus and attention. Engaging in phone conversations, reading or sending texts or emails, or using apps all involve significant cognitive workload that removes much of a driver's attention from actually operating the vehicle. Numerous studies have found that driving while distracted by a phone is just as dangerous as - if not more dangerous than - driving while intoxicated. 

Allowing any cell phone use also opens the door for increasingly distracted behavior over time. Hands-free options like Bluetooth enable more lengthy phone conversations while driving, but conversations still divert mental focus. Texting while stopped at red lights could become more widespread and lead to multitasking even while driving. A total ban helps set a clear boundary that phones have no place in the driver's seat.

Instead of cell phone use, the safest option is for drivers to fully focus their eyes, hands, and mind on the task of driving. This protects not just the driver, but also other people sharing the road, whether in other vehicles, on bikes, or as pedestrians. A total ban on cell phone use while driving is prudent policy to help prevent accidents and promote public safety on our roads. Drivers should abstain from cell phone use until safely parked.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my support for the Electoral College. I believe that this system is the best way to ensure that the President of the United States is elected by a broad coalition of voters, and not just by a handful of states with large populations.

I grew up in a small town in the Midwest. My town was a microcosm of America, with people from all walks of life. We had farmers, teachers, doctors, lawyers, and everything in between. We all had different political views, but we all shared a common bond: we were all Americans.

When it came time to vote for President, my town was always a battleground. The Democrats and Republicans would each put up a candidate, and we would all go to the polls and cast our votes. Sometimes the Democrat would win, and sometimes the Republican would win. But no matter who won, we all knew that the President had been elected by the people, not by a handful of big cities.

I believe that the Electoral College is the best way to ensure that the President is elected by the people. It prevents a few big cities from deciding who becomes President, and it gives smaller states a voice in the process.

I know that there are some people who argue that the Electoral College is outdated and should be abolished. They say that it is unfair that a person can win the popular vote but still lose the election. However, I believe that the Electoral College is a necessary safeguard against tyranny of the majority. It prevents a small number of states from controlling the outcome of the election, and it ensures that all Americans have a say in who becomes President.

I urge you to vote against any proposal to abolish the Electoral College. The Electoral College is a vital part of our democracy, and it should be preserved.

Sincerely,

A Concerned Citizen

Summer projects assigned to students should be student-designed rather than teacher-designed. While teacher-designed projects aim to continue classroom learning over the summer, student-designed projects allow for more freedom and creativity. 

If projects are designed by teachers, students have little say in the topics they research or activities they complete. This can feel less like an exploratory learning experience and more like an assignment to check off a list. In contrast, student-designed projects empower students to follow their interests and dive deeper into subjects they personally find engaging. For example, a student interested in science may choose to conduct backyard observations of local wildlife over the summer rather than following a prescribed lab experiment.

Student ownership over summer projects also fosters greater motivation. When students get to choose their own path of inquiry, they are more likely to fully engage with the material. The desire to learn comes from within, rather than feeling like an externally mandated chore. Seeing the fruits of their own exploration may even inspire students to further extend their learning independently after the initial project is completed. 

Of course, teacher guidance still has an important place. Educators can provide parameters for project topics, suggest learning resources, and be available for consultation. But the specifics of each student's work should be self-directed. Overall, summer projects that emerge from student interests and ideas, rather than being teacher-assigned, are more conducive to meaningful learning experiences during the school break.

In order to keep people connected to the world around them, technology can be a helpful tool, but humans must not allow it to limit their contact with other people.

As an eighth-grade student, I am constantly thinking about my future and the path I want to take. Additionally, some employers or colleges may view a three-year diploma as less impressive than a four-year one, which could impact a student's chances of getting hired or accepted into a program.

Overall, while graduating in three years can certainly be a quick and cost-effective way to earn a high school diploma, it's important for students to carefully consider the pros and cons before making a decision. ## The Advantages of Limiting Car Usage

In recent years, there has been a growing movement to limit car usage. This movement is driven by a number of factors, including the environmental impact of cars, the cost of car ownership, and the health risks associated with driving.

One of the most important reasons to limit car usage is the environmental impact of cars. Cars are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, which contribute to climate change. In addition, cars pollute the air and water, and they contribute to noise pollution.

Another reason to limit car usage is the cost of car ownership. Cars are expensive to purchase, maintain, and insure. In addition, the cost of gasoline has been rising steadily in recent years. This makes it difficult for many people to afford to own a car.

Finally, driving can be dangerous. Car accidents are a leading cause of death and injury in the United States. In addition, driving can be stressful and can lead to health problems such as obesity and heart disease.

There are a number of ways to limit car usage. One way is to walk or bike instead of driving whenever possible. Another way is to take public transportation. Many cities have excellent public transportation systems that can take people anywhere they need to go. In addition, there are a number of car-sharing services available in many cities. These services allow people to rent a car when they need it, rather than owning one.

Limiting car usage can have a number of benefits. It can help to reduce air pollution, noise pollution, and traffic congestion. It can also save people money on gas, car insurance, and car maintenance. In addition, it can make people healthier by encouraging them to walk or bike more.

There are a few challenges to limiting car usage. One challenge is that many people do not have access to public transportation or car-sharing services. Another challenge is that some people do not like to walk or bike. However, there are a number of ways to overcome these challenges. For example, cities can build more sidewalks and bike lanes to make it easier for people to walk or bike. In addition, car-sharing companies can expand their services to more areas.

Limiting car usage is a win-win for everyone. It is good for the environment, it is good for people's health, and it can save people money. If we all make an effort to limit our car usage, we can make a real difference in the world.

Summer Projects

Public school years are designed to give teachers and students two months off as a summer vacation. Many do not like this format. They think students forget too much of the material they learned over the school year. To combat this, schools are starting to introduce summer projects. These projects are designed to maintain the levels of education students have received. However, schools are having trouble introducing these projects. They can not decide who should be able to design them. Some think teachers should, while others believe students should. Students should design their projects in order for them to get the most educational value out of the assignment.

Summer is a time for students to sleep in and be care free. Many do not like the idea of completing a summer project. They think that their freedom is being taken away. Allowing students to design their project will increase their motivation. Most of the time, they will have chosen a topic that interests them. The project will not be put off until the end of summer. Being interested in a subject sparks a need to learn more. They will constantly want to learn more about the subject matter. Each new fact will increase the complexity of the project. The knowledge gained from excess research will provide a basis for their next year in school.

A student that voluntarily researches has more than just motivation. They have a thirst for knowledge. This thirst will motivate them to put more effort into their projects. The effort they put in will help to create a substantial project. The knowledge they gain will not disappear. It will be engraved in their brains for years to come. Each project will help them to learn time management skills and organization strategies as well. These skills will help students grow as individuals. They will help students be successful in college and in their lives after school.

Sometimes students are busy. Those that are involved in sports and clubs, and might not have a lot of time to complete a summer project. In this case, they can choose a project similar to a classmate. The two students will be able to make the project easier to complete. They are able to coordinate with each other, and split up responsibilities. They will have to do two separate projects, but the work will not be as hard. They will also learn how to work together as a team. Learning how to share responsibilities and be a team player will also help them in their lives after school. Careers require teamwork skills, hard work, and reliability.

Although letting students have control over their projects would keep them interested and motivated, some worry that the project might not have the right educational value. Letting teachers design the project will ensure the students are getting the right amount of learning. The rubric and content will be specific to certain classes or subjects. Teachers can make sure specific subjects are being covered if they are responsible for creating each project. The projects could also prepare students for upcoming classes. They will learn basic knowledge needed to be prepared for higher level classes. The project could prepare students for the future school year.

Schools that have implemented a summer project are trying to prevent loss of knowledge. During summer, students forget a lot of the knowledge learned from the previous school year. Allowing students to design their summer projects will help reduce this loss of knowledge. They will become more motivated, learn more about the subject they are interested in, and learn valuable life lessons. Letting their teachers design the projects will guarantee educational value, but the students will benefit more from choosing their own. No one wants to be forced to complete something during their free time. Students that choose their own project will not look at it as an assignment, but as a time to learn more.

While summer is a time meant for rest and relaxation, having some structured learning over the break can help students retain knowledge and develop skills. When it comes to assigning summer projects, I believe giving students some choice and autonomy in designing their own projects strikes the best balance.

Student-designed projects allow individuals to pursue topics that genuinely interest them. This makes the work feel less like a chore and more like an engaging way to spend free time. If students had control over their project topics, they would be intrinsically motivated to dive deeply into learning something new. They could choose to further explore a subject already studied during the school year or investigate an area completely outside the usual curriculum. Having this freedom and control over their education empowers students.

However, teacher guidance is still important to ensure projects have educational merit. Teachers could provide parameters for project scope and content to keep students on track. They could also approve topic ideas to steer clear of subjects inappropriate for schoolwork. With teacher approval of the overall concept, students then scope and carry out the project themselves. This provides structure while still giving independence. 

Student choice also fosters responsibility. By designing their own project guidelines and deadlines, students face real consequences if they fail to follow through. This mimics the independent work environment in college and careers. Meeting self-imposed expectations and staying on schedule for a self-designed project builds important time management skills.

In conclusion, the best summer project system balances student freedom and teacher oversight. Allowing students to choose their own topics within school-approved guidelines empowers independent learning. It also cultivates motivation, responsibility and real-world skills that will serve students well in their educational careers and beyond.

Student learning isn't over at the end of any given school year. Many schools require students to do schoolwork over the summer, like research or projects. Recently, some schools have allowed the students themselves to design the project they want to complete. While student designed projects have seen mixed results, they beg the question of whether students or teachers are better are designing projects for learning over summer break. While student-designed projects allow for a bit more creativity, it is clear that teachers should design projects because they have more knowledge about how to design projects, they describe to students how to complete said project, and they are more likely to design the project purely to help the student learn.

Summer projects designed by a teacher are created so that students can learn the material over break. Seeing how all teachers have a degree in teaching, they have a lot of knowledge on how to create a good assignment in certain scenarios. Even if they did not, they would still know more than the average student due to their experience in the classroom. A good example of a summer project done right is the summer assignment for incoming Generic_School freshmen. When they get accepted, they receive a few books in a package welcoming them to the university. They are then supposed to read the books over the summer so they can have a discussion with the author of the books when they get to school in the fall. While getting the author of a book is probably unreasonable for most high schools, it would be very easy to have students discuss the books in a seminar during the first two weeks of school.

When teachers grade projects, many follow a certain grading rubric to decide what grade a certain student has received on an assignment. However if a student designed a project, it would likely be much harder to grade for the teachers and complete for the students. A student designed project may have a messy grading rubric, a rubric that only grades off of completion, or even no rubric at all, opting for students to create a project with few guidelines. While such rubrics may create more chance of creativity due to a lack of specificity, more times than not it will only to the students not knowing what they are supposed to do to get a good grade. Speaking from personal experiences in school, it's incredibly frustrating when you don't know what you need to do on an assignment to get a good grade. Teachers would also have a bad time grading student designed projects, as it is harder to grade an assignment if they don't know what aspects of learning to grade or how to grade them. It would be better for a teacher to design a project so students know what to do in a project and teachers know how to grade it.

When designing a summer project, students would be at the end of a school year and burnt out with learning. When faced with another project at the end of the year, many students may lazily design projects that are easy to complete. Some examples of an easy project include reading a book without annotations or comprehension or creating a small research project that could be completed in a day. Although said projects could easily earn good grades, they don't help the student in learning the material over the break. If the students do not learn the material over break, then it defeats the purpose of having a project over summer break. An easy project with no nuance is a waste of time for everyone involved, as the teachers don't teach the student anything and students don't learn anything.

Learning material over the summer is important for students. Without it, many of them would forget the material over the break and come into the new school year completely empty headed. Teacher designed projects are by far the best way for students to learn new things over summer break. Although projects don't need to take up a majority of someone's time in the summer, a small amount of learning would allow students to take a much needed break while still retaining what they know from the previous year. Keeping the material in their head over the summer will help students become better learners. Helping students become better learners will help them succeed both in school and life.

While extracurricular activities provide benefits to students, mandating participation risks overburdening some. Here is a balanced perspective:

Extracurricular activities can enhance the high school experience when chosen voluntarily. Sports, arts and service clubs cultivate valuable skills like collaboration, time management and leadership. Such experiences complement academics, helping students discover passions and build confidence. 

However, mandating participation risks unfairly burdening some students. Those with responsibilities outside school, such as caring for family members, may have little free time. Others must work part-time jobs to support themselves or their families financially. Forcing extra commitments onto those with heavy work or home life obligations could cause unnecessary stress.

Instead of a mandate, the principal could encourage involvement through promotion of opportunities and outreach to find each student's strengths. Students feeling overextended by academics could benefit from reduced course-loads in exchange for extracurricular commitments. Participation requirements could exempt those demonstrating lack of available time or energy. 

Overall, extracurricular activities offer benefits but should not come at the cost of overburdening some students or undermining personal choices. A balanced approach that accounts for differing student circumstances would be preferable to an outright mandate. Encouragement of involvement through promoting opportunities, instead of requirements, respects students' agency while helping them engage in enriching activities.

Finally, the article points out that there are many other faces on Mars, all of which are natural landforms. This suggests that the Face is not unique and is therefore not likely to be the product of alien intelligence.

First impressions are often seen as set in stone, with little room for change. However, I believe that this is a misconception. While first impressions can be difficult to alter, they are not impossible to change. In fact, with effort and awareness, individuals can work to overcome negative first impressions and form more positive ones.

One of the reasons why first impressions can be difficult to change is because they are often based on superficial factors. For example, someone may make a negative first impression based on a person's appearance, body language, or accent. However, these factors may not accurately reflect a person's true character or personality. By recognizing that first impressions are often based on superficial factors, individuals can work to overcome negative first impressions by getting to know the person on a deeper level.

Additionally, first impressions can be influenced by a person's own biases and prejudices. For example, someone may make a negative first impression of someone based on their race or ethnicity, without even realizing it. By becoming aware of their own biases and working to overcome them, individuals can work to form more positive first impressions.

In my experience, I have seen first impressions change over time. For example, when I first met someone at a party, I may have formed a negative first impression based on their appearance or behavior. However, as I got to know them better, I may have discovered that they were actually very kind and caring individuals. By recognizing that first impressions can change over time, individuals can work to overcome negative first impressions and form more positive ones.

In conclusion, while first impressions can be difficult to change, they are not impossible. By recognizing that first impressions are often based on superficial factors and can be influenced by biases and prejudices, individuals can work to overcome negative first impressions and form more positive ones. With effort and awareness, individuals can create a more positive and inclusive environment for themselves and others.

While the Facial Action Coding System technology described in the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile" aims to help teachers understand their students' emotions, its use to read student expressions in the classroom raises some valid concerns. 

On one hand, this technology could allow teachers to gain valuable insights into how their lessons and instruction are affecting students. If a teacher notices many students appear bored or confused during a certain part of a lesson, it could prompt the teacher to find new ways to engage the class or reexplain a difficult concept. Identifying specific students who seem frustrated may also help teachers provide additional support to those struggling with the material. 

However, there are also significant downsides to constantly monitoring student emotions this way. Students should feel comfortable freely expressing a range of natural human emotions like confusion, frustration, or disinterest in class without fearing the teacher may misinterpret their facial expressions. Constantly having their emotions read and analyzed could add unnecessary pressure and stress. Students may also feel a loss of privacy and that they are being treated more like subjects in an experiment than individuals. 

Overall, while the intent of using this technology is to help improve teaching and learning, the negatives likely outweigh the positives. Teachers should focus on building strong relationships with students so they feel comfortable directly communicating how they are feeling about lessons, rather than relying on computers to interpret subtle facial cues. While the Facial Action Coding System shows potential to provide insights, monitoring students this closely on a daily basis risks compromising their well-being and autonomy in the classroom. For these reasons, its broad use does not seem prudent or valuable at this time.

I disagree with the principal's decision that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While extracurriculars provide many benefits, mandatory participation should not be imposed on students. 

Extracurricular activities can be very rewarding for those who voluntarily choose to participate. They allow students to explore interests, learn new skills, build confidence and develop important virtues like teamwork. However, mandatory participation risks overriding individual interests and circumstances. Some students may need to prioritize academic studies due to familial responsibilities or personal challenges. Others may not enjoy group activities or prefer solitary hobbies. Forcing involvement denies students' autonomy over personal choices and schedules.

A "one-size-fits-all" policy also fails to accommodate diversity of skills, talents and ambitions among the student body. Not all find motivation in sports, arts or leadership roles. A mandatory requirement might cause frustration or lack of interest for those in activities that do not align with their passions or strengths. It is better to encourage participation through promotion of benefits, rather than imposition through force. Students are more likely to invest fully and gain maximum rewards from voluntary participation in areas that inspire their commitment and enthusiasm. 

Instead of mandating extracurriculars, the principal could consider alternatives that respect students' agency while still supporting engagement. For example, providing flexible options so every individual can discover at least one activity they truly enjoy. Offering school clubs related to diverse interests like languages, technology or hobbies. Recognizing accomplishments not only in sports/arts but also academic/service achievements done independently. This balanced approach empowers students to choose rewarding involvement through their own motivated exploration, respecting personal goals and circumstances.

In conclusion, while extracurricular activities offer valuable benefits, mandatory uniform participation policies risk violating students' autonomy and fail to account for diverse individual circumstances. It is better to encourage voluntary involvement through flexible promotion of options, interests and rewards, allowing each student to connect in areas aligned with their unique skills, passions and priorities for development. For these reasons, I do not support requiring all students to participate in at least one extracurricular.
